parts.title: Sentence comprehension: Folk night note
parts.instructions: Read the short email from a friend. Choose the best word for each gap (1-5).
parts.passage:
Hi Leo,

I wanted to tell you about the acoustic folk evening I went to at the harbour café last Friday. Even though the venue was quite small, the sound quality [1] out to be much clearer than I had expected. The lead guitarist [2] us not to talk near the stage because the microphones pick up every whisper. Halfway through the set, she invited a local fiddle player to join in, [3] made the whole room feel like a traditional festival. Afterwards, I bought one of their vinyl records, [4] the fact that I still need to repair my old turntable at home. You should definitely come [5] with me next month if they announce another date!

Best,
Astrid

questions.explanation: 'Turned out to be' is the phrasal verb meaning happened or proved to be in the end; 'worked out' and 'proved' do not take 'out to be' here.
'Reminded us not to talk' fits the pattern verb + object + not to + infinitive; 'suggested' and 'explained' cannot take 'us not to talk'.
'Which' introduces a non-defining relative clause after a comma referring to the whole previous clause.
'Despite the fact that' is a preposition phrase followed by a noun phrase ('the fact that'); 'although' and 'however' cannot precede 'the fact that' directly.
'Come along with me' means to accompany someone to an event; 'across' and 'around' do not fit this invitation.

parts.title: Opinion matching: Collecting vinyl records
parts.instructions: Four people (A-D) give their opinions about buying and listening to vinyl records. Match each statement (1-7) to the correct person. You can use each person more than once.

texts.title: Astrid
texts.text: I started buying second-hand vinyl records when I moved into a flat near a weekend street market. For me, the biggest attraction is the large cardboard sleeve with lyrics and photographs printed inside, which you never get with a digital playlist. New releases can be quite expensive, so I rarely pay full price in city-centre shops. Instead, I spend Saturday mornings searching through dusty crates for forgotten folk albums that cost less than a cup of coffee.

texts.title: Leo
texts.text: I stream music on my phone while I am on the bus, because carrying records around is obviously impossible. At home, however, putting a record on the turntable forces me to slow down and listen to an album from the first track to the last without skipping songs. That said, I do wish independent record shops would label their second-hand stock more honestly. Twice I have bought records marked as clean that turned out to have deep scratches.

texts.title: Naomi
texts.text: Unlike some of my friends, I do not collect vinyl because I think the sound is magically better than a good CD. In fact, my small bedroom speakers probably cannot show much difference at all. What I genuinely love is walking into a local record shop and talking to the staff behind the counter. They always remember what bands I like and suggest acoustic artists I would never have discovered on an algorithm.

texts.title: Hamid
texts.text: I used to buy dozens of cheap albums online every year, until I realised I barely played half of them. Now I limit myself to one new vinyl record a month, usually bought directly from a band at the end of a live acoustic concert. Paying twenty-five pounds feels steep compared with a streaming subscription, yet I know almost all of that money goes straight to the musicians rather than a big platform.

parts.title: Long text comprehension: Acoustic sessions and vinyl
parts.instructions: Read the article about intimate acoustic concerts and the return of vinyl records. Match each paragraph (1-7) to the best heading (A-H). There is one extra heading that you do not need.

paragraphs.text: Long before electric guitars and stadium loudspeakers existed, folk songs travelled from village to village through live voices and simple wooden instruments. Musicians gathered in kitchens, harbour taverns, and town halls, where audiences sat close enough to hear every breath and string vibration. Because there were no microphones, singers learned to project clearly while keeping stories at the heart of each tune. Even today, that direct connection between performer and listener remains the main reason acoustic music feels so personal.

When recorded sound first entered ordinary homes in the twentieth century, flat black vinyl discs quickly became the standard way to hear music outside a concert hall. Families saved up to buy a single record player for the living room and shared favourite albums after dinner. Pressing sound waves into physical grooves was a clever yet delicate process, and listeners soon learned to hold discs carefully by the edges so fingerprints and dust would not ruin a treasured recording.

By the late nineteen-eighties, shiny compact discs and later digital downloads appeared to push vinyl off the shelves for good. Record factories closed down, and second-hand shops filled up with unwanted boxes of LPs sold for pennies. Digital files were smaller, never scratched in a backpack, and let people carry thousands of songs in one pocket. Most industry experts predicted that turntables would soon belong only in history museums.

Instead of disappearing, however, vinyl records experienced a remarkable comeback over the past fifteen years. Curious teenagers began buying turntables alongside older collectors who missed holding a physical album. At the same time, listeners tired of huge, noisy festival crowds started seeking out tiny 'house concerts' and quiet back-room acoustic nights. Both trends share the same wish: to treat music as a focused experience rather than background noise while checking emails.

Running a small acoustic venue brings practical challenges that big arena promoters never face. Without loud drums or heavy amplification, even the clink of coffee cups or a ringing phone can spoil a quiet ballad. Venue organisers therefore ask guests to switch off screens before the first song and often seat latecomers only between tracks. In return, artists frequently step off the low stage after the show to chat with listeners and sign record sleeves.

This renewed demand has created unexpected delays for independent musicians who want to release their acoustic sessions on vinyl. Only a limited number of pressing plants still operate worldwide, and major pop stars often book months of factory time in advance. As a result, a local folk singer who records a live album in spring might wait until winter before receiving two hundred copies to sell at concerts.

Looking ahead, engineers and environmentally minded musicians are testing cleaner ways to keep physical music alive. Traditional vinyl is made from oil-based plastic, which requires high heat and energy to mould. Several European factories have begun pressing records from recycled plastics or plant-based materials, while acoustic clubs encourage fans to travel by train and bring reusable cups. These small changes suggest that classic listening habits can adapt to a greener future.

headings: Why digital formats nearly replaced physical discs
Practical rules that protect quiet live performances
How stadium tours became cheaper for young bands
Production queues slow down independent releases
How acoustic music first brought listeners together
Greener materials for future records and clubs
The early arrival of records in family homes
A shared return to slower, focused listening

gaps.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes how early folk musicians played without microphones in small community spaces, creating a direct connection with listeners.
Paragraph 2 explains how vinyl discs entered family living rooms in the twentieth century and how listeners learned to care for them.
Paragraph 3 covers how CDs and digital files offered convenience and durability, leading experts to think vinyl would vanish.
Paragraph 4 links the return of vinyl and small acoustic nights to people wanting a focused musical experience rather than background noise.
Paragraph 5 outlines the quiet-room etiquette—switching off phones and seating latecomers between songs—needed at small acoustic venues.
Paragraph 6 explains how limited pressing plants and major-label bookings force independent folk artists to wait months for their records.
Paragraph 7 discusses recycled plastics, plant-based discs, and greener travel habits at acoustic clubs.

parts.title: Monologue comprehension
parts.instructions: Listen to two speakers giving short talks: first an acoustic guitarist about recording a live album (questions 1-2), then a record shop owner about running a small independent store (questions 3-4). Choose the best answer for each question.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: First, you will hear Eve, an acoustic guitarist, talking about recording her first live vinyl album in a small harbour hall.

turns.speaker: eve
turns.text: When my label suggested recording a live album, most people assumed I would book a modern city studio and invite fifty fans to clap between songs. Actually, I chose an old wooden hall by the harbour because the natural echo made my guitar sound warm without any digital effects. I worried beforehand that passing seagulls or a creaking floorboard might spoil the quiet ballads. In the end, those tiny background sounds became my favourite part of the record — they remind listeners that a real evening happened there. What genuinely surprised me, though, was how differently I played in front of a microphone that couldn't be edited later. Instead of rushing through tricky guitar parts like I sometimes do at concerts, I slowed down and stayed calm on every single chorus.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Now you will hear Miles, who has run an independent record shop for twelve years.

turns.speaker: miles
turns.text: Customers often picture me sitting behind the counter all day drinking coffee and listening to classic folk records. While I certainly play plenty of great music, half my week is actually spent cleaning dusty boxes of donated vinyl and checking every disc under a bright lamp for tiny scratches. If you miss a single jump on a needle, an unhappy buyer won't come back. People also ask whether online superstores have hurt my business. Oddly enough, the internet helped us survive by letting us post short audio clips of rare records we stock. Even so, my best tip for anyone thinking of opening a music shop is simple: host free Sunday afternoon acoustic sets inside the store. Once neighbours step through the door for a live song, they usually browse the shelves and become regular customers.

parts.title: Personal experience and discussion
parts.instructions: You have 1 minute to prepare and 2 minutes to speak continuously. Answer all three questions in one organised talk.

topics.prompt:
Talk about a song, album, or live performance that means a lot to you. Answer all three questions in one 2-minute talk:
1. Tell me about a memorable musical experience you had in the past.
2. How did the music make you feel at that moment, and why?
3. Why do you think physical formats like vinyl records remain popular in the digital age?
